lessons.title: Unit 4: Indices, standard form and surds
lessons.content:
For non-zero a, aᵐ×aⁿ=aᵐ⁺ⁿ, aᵐ/aⁿ=aᵐ⁻ⁿ and (aᵐ)ⁿ=aᵐⁿ. A negative index means reciprocal: a⁻ⁿ=1/aⁿ. Standard form writes a number as A×10ⁿ where 1≤|A|<10. A surd is an irrational root such as √2; simplify by taking out perfect-square factors, for example √72=6√2.

Check restrictions before cancelling algebraic factors, and keep exact surd values until the final step.

lessons.title: Unit 5: Statistics, probability and interpretation
lessons.content:
A population is the whole group being studied; a sample is a selected subset. Mean is total divided by number of observations, median is the middle ordered value, and mode is the most frequent value. Range is maximum minus minimum. Choose a graph that suits the data: bar charts compare categories, histograms show grouped continuous data, and line graphs show change over time.

For equally likely outcomes, P(A)=number of favourable outcomes/total outcomes. Probability lies between 0 and 1. Use a representative sample and avoid conclusions that the data cannot support.

lessons.title: Unit 4: Quadratic equations and discriminant
lessons.content:
A quadratic equation has the form ax²+bx+c=0, a≠0. Factorisation solves it by expressing the quadratic as a product of linear factors. The quadratic formula is x=[−b±√(b²−4ac)]/(2a). The discriminant D=b²−4ac predicts the roots: D>0 gives two distinct real roots, D=0 one repeated real root, and D<0 no real roots.

Substitute each root into the original equation to check it. In applications, define the variable and reject roots that do not fit the context.

lessons.title: Unit 5: Trigonometry and mensuration applications
lessons.content:
For an acute angle θ in a right triangle, sinθ=opposite/hypotenuse, cosθ=adjacent/hypotenuse and tanθ=opposite/adjacent. Use the ratio that connects the known side to the required side. Bearings, heights and distances require a labelled diagram and a clearly identified angle.

Area of a triangle is ½bh; circle area is πr² and circumference is 2πr. Cylinder volume is πr²h. Keep units consistent and distinguish area units from volume units.

lessons.title: Unit 4: Arithmetic and geometric sequences
lessons.content:
An arithmetic sequence has a constant difference d. Its nth term is aₙ=a₁+(n−1)d and the sum of n terms is Sₙ=n/2[2a₁+(n−1)d]. A geometric sequence has a constant ratio r; its nth term is aₙ=a₁rⁿ⁻¹. For r≠1, Sₙ=a₁(1−rⁿ)/(1−r).

Identify whether differences or ratios are constant before selecting a formula. Check the first few terms and ensure the requested term number is correct.

lessons.title: Unit 5: Vectors and binomial theorem
lessons.content:
A vector has magnitude and direction. In two dimensions, a=(aₓ,aᵧ); addition is component-wise and |a|=√(aₓ²+aᵧ²). The dot product is a·b=|a||b|cosθ=aₓbₓ+aᵧbᵧ and is useful for finding angles and projections.

The binomial theorem expands (a+b)ⁿ using coefficients nCr. The general term is nCr aⁿ⁻ʳbʳ. Track powers carefully and check that the powers of each term add to n.

lessons.title: Unit 4: Applications of differentiation
lessons.content:
The derivative f′(x) is the instantaneous rate of change and the gradient of the tangent to y=f(x). If f′(x)>0 the function is increasing locally; if f′(x)<0 it is decreasing. Stationary points occur where f′(x)=0. The second derivative can help classify a stationary point: f″(x)>0 indicates a local minimum and f″(x)<0 a local maximum when the test applies.

For optimisation, define the quantity to maximise or minimise, express it as a function of one variable, find stationary points and check endpoints and the context.

lessons.title: Unit 5: Integration, differential equations and probability
lessons.content:
Integration reverses differentiation. ∫xⁿdx=xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)+C for n≠−1. A definite integral gives signed area under a curve between limits. Differential equations relate a function to its derivatives and model changing quantities such as growth or motion.

For independent events A and B, P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). For mutually exclusive events, P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B). Read wording carefully: independent and mutually exclusive are different ideas.
